paragraphs.text: Autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia-51 is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder caused by deficiency of the adaptor protein complex-4 (AP-4). It begins with infantile hypotonia that progresses to spasticity, either spastic paraplegia or spastic tetraplegia. Other features are microcephaly, severe intellectual disability, absent or very limited speech, inability to walk, stereotypic laughter, drooling, and growth retardation. Some patients have seizures. Moreno-De-Luca et al. (2011) first described the disorder as an autosomal recessive form of spastic tetraplegic cerebral palsy. Because disruption of different AP-4 subunits produces similar phenotypes, Moreno-De-Luca et al. (2011), Abou Jamra et al. (2011), and Kong et al. (2013) regarded it as part of a clinically recognizable 'AP-4 deficiency syndrome'.

paragraphs.text: Moreno-De-Luca et al. (2011) reported 2 sibs from a consanguineous Palestinian-Jordanian family with a neurologic condition that had been described as cerebral palsy. The female proband was born at term after an uneventful labor and delivery. She had microcephaly and hypotonia at birth, which progressed to spastic tetraplegia with hyperreflexia and generalized hypertonia by the first year of life. She never developed speech or independent walking. From 5 years of age she was wheelchair-bound and had generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Examination at age 23 showed microcephaly (-3 SD), profoundly impaired cognition, adaptive skills at age equivalents below 1 year, drooling, and outbursts of stereotypic laughter. Dysmorphic features included bitemporal narrowing, a long narrow face with a prominent pointed chin, downslanting palpebral fissures, a long nose with a wide nasal ridge, a short philtrum with an everted full upper vermilion, prominent antehelix of the ears, and facial hypotonia. Brain MRI showed ventriculomegaly, cortical and cerebellar atrophy, reduced hippocampal volume, and diffuse white matter loss, most pronounced in the frontal region and corpus callosum. EEG showed generalized theta slowing. Her brother had microcephaly and hypotonia after birth, and developmental delay was evident by the first year of life. He acquired a few dysarthric words and could walk with support, but increasing spasticity made him wheelchair-dependent by age 9 years. His seizures began as staring spells and became generalized tonic-clonic at age 15. At age 22 he had spastic tetraplegia with hypertonia and hyperreflexia, stereotypic laughter, drooling, jerky nystagmus, and severe cognitive deficits. Head CT showed moderate ventriculomegaly. Both sibs had a Babinski sign, no sphincter control, and normal eye and hearing evaluations. The authors noted that the clinical features closely resembled those of a family with an AP4M1 mutation.

Features included severe intellectual disability, absent speech, shy character, stereotypic laughter, and muscular hypotonia that progressed to spastic paraplegia. Patients also had microcephaly, foot deformity, decreased muscle mass of the lower limbs, inability to walk, and growth retardation.

paragraphs.text: Kong et al. (2013) reported identical twin girls born to first-cousin Moroccan parents. The pregnancy was uncomplicated, but neonatal asphyxiation was noted at delivery. At age 3 years both twins had marked developmental retardation with microcephaly (head circumference -2 SD and -2.5 SD), inability to walk unaided, abnormal speech, and abnormal circadian development. Other features were smiling or laughing for no obvious reason, drooling, muscular hypotonia, short stature, and low body weight. Neurologic examination showed spastic paraplegia of the lower extremities without hyperreflexia or Babinski sign. Neither twin had seizures, and sphincter control was absent. Both had a prominent, bulbous nose, a wide mouth, and coarse features. EEG showed diffuse slow waves, and CT showed atrophy of the inferior vermis with cortical atrophy. One twin had conductive hearing loss on the left side. The twins were diagnosed with type I complex hereditary spastic paraplegia. Both had also been vaccinated with BCG a few days after birth. At 9 months of age each developed unilaterally enlarged, inflamed axillary lymph nodes containing acid-fast bacilli. No abnormality of the IL-12/IFN-gamma axis or of the oxidative burst was found.

paragraphs.text: The transmission pattern of SPG51 is autosomal recessive. Moreno-De-Luca et al. (2011) found affected sibs in a consanguineous family who were homozygous for an AP4E1-containing deletion, and their unaffected mother was a heterozygous carrier. Abou Jamra et al. (2011) and Kong et al. (2013) also reported consanguineous families with homozygous AP4E1 mutations. In the family reported by Kong et al. (2013), both parents were heterozygous for the mutation.

paragraphs.text: Moreno-De-Luca et al. (2011) performed chromosomal microarray analysis in 2 sibs with spastic tetraplegia, intellectual disability, microcephaly, and epilepsy from a consanguineous Palestinian-Jordanian family. Both sibs were homozygous for a 192-kb deletion on chromosome 15q21.2 that included the 5-prime ends of the AP4E1 and SPPL2A genes. The deletion was confirmed by FISH. The mother was a heterozygous carrier, and methylation analysis indicated that the father was also a carrier. The authors could not completely exclude a contribution from SPPL2A deletion, but they proposed that AP4E1 deficiency was the main cause of the phenotype. They also proposed that disruption of any of the 4 AP-4 subunits abolishes the function of the complex.

In one family they found a homozygous splice site mutation in the AP4E1 gene (c.542+1_542+4delGTAA). The mutation caused deletion of r.421_542 and was predicted to result in a frameshift (p.Glu181GlyfsTer20). In the other 2 families they found mutations in the AP4S1 and AP4B1 genes.

paragraphs.text: Kong et al. (2013) performed whole-exome sequencing in Moroccan identical twins with complex spastic paraplegia and BCG disease. They found a homozygous nonsense mutation in the AP4E1 gene (R1105X), which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Both parents were heterozygous for the mutation and a healthy sib was wildtype. The mutation was not found in 1,050 CEPH controls or in 69 Moroccan controls. In patient cells, AP4E1 mRNA levels and splicing were normal. However, the AP-4-epsilon protein was barely detectable, and levels of the AP-4-mu and AP-4-beta subunits were also reduced. Native immunoprecipitation showed that levels of assembled AP-4 complex were more than 95% lower in patient fibroblasts and EBV-transformed B cells than in controls. The AP-4 binding partner tepsin was not detectable in patient fibroblasts. Kong et al. (2013) found no defects in known genes for mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease (MSMD) and proposed that the AP4E1 mutation was the most likely cause of the twins' mycobacterial disease.

checks.claim: Kong et al. (2013) performed whole-exome sequencing in Moroccan identical twins with complex spastic paraplegia and BCG disease.
checks.evidence_quote: We used WES to search for genetic lesions in these twins with both neurological and immunological disorders.
checks.explanation: WES was performed on P1 (an identical twin); the twins had BCG lymphadenitis.

checks.claim: Kong et al. (2013) found a homozygous nonsense mutation in the AP4E1 gene (R1105X) in the Moroccan twins.
checks.evidence_quote: Whole-exome sequencing (WES) revealed a homozygous nonsense mutation (p.R1105X) of the AP4E1 gene, which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

checks.claim: The AP4E1 R1105X mutation was confirmed by Sanger sequencing.
checks.evidence_quote: Whole-exome sequencing (WES) revealed a homozygous nonsense mutation (p.R1105X) of the AP4E1 gene, which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

checks.claim: Both parents of the Moroccan twins were heterozygous for the AP4E1 R1105X mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: both P1 and P2 carried the same homozygous mutation, whereas the parents were heterozygous and a healthy sibling was wild-type at this locus

checks.claim: A healthy sib of the Moroccan twins was wildtype for AP4E1 R1105X.
checks.evidence_quote: both P1 and P2 carried the same homozygous mutation, whereas the parents were heterozygous and a healthy sibling was wild-type at this locus

checks.claim: The AP4E1 R1105X mutation was not found in 1,050 CEPH controls.
checks.evidence_quote: This variant was not found in the sequences of 1,050 healthy controls from 51 ethnic groups from the Centre d'Étude du Polymorphisme Humain (CEPH) panel [35], [36] or in an additional 69 Moroccan controls.

checks.claim: The AP4E1 R1105X mutation was not found in 69 Moroccan controls.
checks.evidence_quote: This variant was not found in the sequences of 1,050 healthy controls from 51 ethnic groups from the Centre d'Étude du Polymorphisme Humain (CEPH) panel [35], [36] or in an additional 69 Moroccan controls.

checks.claim: In cells from the Moroccan twins with AP4E1 R1105X, AP4E1 mRNA levels and splicing were normal.
checks.evidence_quote: the RT-qPCR and RT-PCR results suggest that the homozygous p.R1105X mutation had no qualitative or quantitative effect on AP4E1 gene transcription, at least in EBV-B cells.

checks.claim: In cells from the Moroccan twins with AP4E1 R1105X, the AP-4-epsilon protein was barely detectable.
checks.evidence_quote: AP-4ε was barely detectable in EBV-B cells from P1, but was clearly present in control cells (Figure 2C).

checks.claim: In cells from the Moroccan twins with AP4E1 R1105X, levels of the AP-4-mu and AP-4-beta subunits were reduced.
checks.evidence_quote: the loss of AP-4ε resulted in a concomitant decrease in the levels of both the AP-4 μ and AP-4β proteins in the patient’s cells.

checks.claim: Native immunoprecipitation showed that levels of assembled AP-4 complex were more than 95% lower in fibroblasts and EBV-transformed B cells from the Moroccan twins than in controls.
checks.evidence_quote: Western-blot analysis showed that the levels of assembled AP-4 were much lower in both fibroblasts and EBV-B cells from P1 than in those from healthy controls (IMAGE J quantification indicated that AP-4 assembly levels were more than 95% lower than those of healthy controls).

checks.claim: The AP-4 binding partner tepsin was not detectable in fibroblasts from the Moroccan twins.
checks.evidence_quote: a recently identified AP-4 binding partner, tepsin, which binds to the C-terminal appendage domain of AP-4β [32], was detectable in control fibroblasts, but not in those of P1 (Figure 3B).

checks.claim: Kong et al. (2013) found no defects in known genes for mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease (MSMD) in the Moroccan twins.
checks.evidence_quote: we identified no genetic or functional defects in the known MSMD-causing genes or IFN-γ/IL-12 axis related genes

checks.claim: Kong et al. (2013) proposed that the AP4E1 R1105X mutation was the most likely cause of the Moroccan twins' mycobacterial disease.
checks.evidence_quote: We thus propose that the AP4E1 mutation is the most likely cause of the mycobacterial disease in our patients.

paragraphs.text: Kong et al. (2018) later restudied the same Moroccan twins, who had both hereditary spastic paraplegia due to the homozygous AP4E1 R1105X mutation and MSMD. Using whole-exome sequencing and genome-wide linkage analysis, they found that the twins were also homozygous for a splice site mutation in the SPPL2A gene (c.733+1G-A). This mutation caused skipping of exon 6. An unrelated Turkish boy with BCG disease was homozygous for a different SPPL2A splice site mutation. Kong et al. (2018) attributed the mycobacterial disease to autosomal recessive SPPL2A deficiency, which led to accumulation of the CD74 N-terminal fragment, depletion of CD1c+ conventional dendritic cells, and impaired IFN-gamma production by mycobacterium-specific memory TH1* cells.

checks.claim: Kong et al. (2018) restudied the Moroccan twins who had hereditary spastic paraplegia due to the homozygous AP4E1 R1105X mutation and MSMD.
checks.evidence_quote: In addition to MSMD, the patients displayed hereditary spastic paraplegia due to a homozygous p.R1105X mutation of the AP4E1 gene.
checks.explanation: The paper describes the Moroccan twins (P1, P2) as having MSMD plus hereditary spastic paraplegia from homozygous AP4E1 p.R1105X; "restudied" is an editorial framing of the same patients.

checks.claim: Using whole-exome sequencing and genome-wide linkage analysis, Kong et al. (2018) found that the Moroccan twins were also homozygous for a splice site mutation in the SPPL2A gene (c.733+1G-A).
checks.evidence_quote: By combining whole-exome sequencing (WES) of P1 and P3 and genome-wide linkage (GWL) for both families, we identified a homozygous essential splice-site mutation in SPPL2A (encoding signal peptide peptidase-like 2A, SPPL2a) in each family
checks.explanation: WES plus genome-wide linkage identified the mutation, and Sanger sequencing confirmed P1 and P2 carried homozygous c.733+1G>A.

checks.claim: The SPPL2A c.733+1G-A mutation caused skipping of exon 6.
checks.evidence_quote: the c.733+1G>A (P1 and P2) mutation was associated with the complete skipping of exon 6 in the encoded mRNA

checks.claim: An unrelated Turkish boy with BCG disease was homozygous for a different SPPL2A splice site mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: a family from Turkey including an affected 11-year-old boy (P3, Kindred B, Fig. 1a). All three children suffered from BCG disease
checks.explanation: P3, an unrelated Turkish boy with BCG disease, carried a homozygous c.1328-1G>A splice acceptor mutation of SPPL2A intron 13, distinct from the twins' mutation.

checks.claim: Kong et al. (2018) attributed the mycobacterial disease to autosomal recessive SPPL2A deficiency.
checks.evidence_quote: We describe here AR complete SPPL2a deficiency, as a genetic etiology of MSMD.
checks.explanation: The authors conclude autosomal recessive SPPL2a deficiency underlies the patients' mycobacterial disease.

checks.claim: SPPL2A deficiency led to accumulation of the CD74 N-terminal fragment.
checks.evidence_quote: The CD74 NTF therefore accumulates in the HLA class II+ myeloid and lymphoid cells of SPPL2a-deficient patients.
checks.explanation: Accumulation of the CD74 N-terminal fragment is demonstrated in patient cells.

checks.claim: SPPL2A deficiency led to depletion of CD1c+ conventional dendritic cells.
checks.evidence_quote: This toxic fragment selectively depletes IL-12- and IL-23-producing CD1c+ conventional dendritic cells (cDC2s) and their circulating progenitors.
checks.explanation: Patients had significantly lower frequencies of CD1c+ cDC2s, a selective loss.

checks.claim: SPPL2A deficiency led to impaired IFN-gamma production by mycobacterium-specific memory TH1* cells.
checks.evidence_quote: SPPL2a-deficient memory TH1* cells selectively fail to produce IFN-γ when stimulated with mycobacterial antigens in vitro
checks.explanation: Impaired IFN-gamma production by mycobacterium-specific memory TH1* cells is a central finding.

The sibs had spastic tetraplegia, profound intellectual disability, microcephaly, epilepsy, and white matter loss. The deletion removed the 5-prime ends of the AP4E1 and SPPL2A genes. It was identified by chromosomal microarray analysis and confirmed by FISH. The mother was a heterozygous carrier, and the father was inferred to be a carrier.

paragraphs.text: Kong et al. (2013) found a homozygous arg1105-to-ter (R1105X) mutation in the AP4E1 gene in identical twin girls born to first-cousin Moroccan parents. The twins had intellectual disability, spastic paraplegia, microcephaly, and short stature. The mutation was identified by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. It segregated with the disorder in the family and was not found in 1,050 CEPH controls or in 69 Moroccan controls. In patient cells, mRNA levels were normal, but AP-4-epsilon protein was barely detectable and assembled AP-4 complex was reduced by more than 95%. The twins also had BCG disease. Kong et al. (2018) later found that they were also homozygous for a splice site mutation in SPPL2A and attributed the mycobacterial disease to SPPL2A deficiency.

checks.evidence_quote: We found only one homozygous nonsense mutation in AP4E1 (Figure 1B, Table 2), resulting in the replacement of an arginine residue in position 1105 with a premature stop codon (p.R1105X).
checks.explanation: The twins are identical, female (Table 1), and born to first-cousin Moroccan parents.

checks.evidence_quote: AP-4ε was barely detectable in EBV-B cells from P1, but was clearly present in control cells (Figure 2C).

checks.evidence_quote: IMAGE J quantification indicated that AP-4 assembly levels were more than 95% lower than those of healthy controls

checks.claim: The Moroccan twins with AP4E1 R1105X also had BCG disease.
checks.evidence_quote: Intriguingly, both children presented with lymphadenitis caused by the live Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine.

checks.claim: Kong et al. (2018) found that the Moroccan twins were also homozygous for a splice site mutation in SPPL2A.
checks.evidence_quote: Sanger sequencing confirmed that both P1 and P2 carried a homozygous c.733+1G>A mutation of the splice donor site of SPPL2A intron 6
checks.explanation: The Moroccan twins were homozygous for an SPPL2A splice-site mutation.

checks.claim: Kong et al. (2018) attributed the mycobacterial disease in the Moroccan twins to SPPL2A deficiency.
checks.evidence_quote: These findings suggest that inherited SPPL2a deficiency in humans underlies mycobacterial disease by decreasing the numbers of cDC2s and impairing IFN-γ production by mycobacterium-specific memory TH1* cells.
checks.explanation: The mycobacterial (BCG) disease in these patients, including the twins, is attributed to SPPL2a deficiency, distinct from the AP4E1-related spastic paraplegia.
